title: Adult cardiac arrest
summary: Adult cardiac arrest resuscitation from first principles, aligned with the 2025 American Heart Association adult basic life support, advanced life support, and post-cardiac arrest care guidelines. This is study material. Care follows the current guideline and local protocol.

principles.title: Coronary and cerebral perfusion depend on compressions
principles.explanation: In cardiac arrest the heart is not producing a pulse, so coronary and cerebral blood flow have to be made from outside. Chest compressions raise aortic pressure. Coronary perfusion pressure, the gradient that fills the coronary arteries, is aortic pressure minus right atrial pressure during the relaxation phase between compressions. Cerebral blood flow also depends on the arterial pressure those compressions generate, and both fall when compressions stop. The 2025 AHA adult cardiac arrest algorithm therefore centers on high-quality compressions: push hard, at least 2 inches (5 cm); push fast, 100 to 120 per minute; let the chest recoil completely; and do not lean on the chest. Full recoil lets the heart refill and lets right atrial pressure fall, which is what keeps the coronary gradient open. Observational data have linked compression depths greater than 6 cm (about 2.4 inches) with lower survival, so the target is at least 5 cm, not as deep as possible. Compress on a firm surface. Depth starts to fall after about 90 to 120 seconds of continuous CPR, which is why the compressor changes about every 2 minutes.

questions.prompt: During CPR, coronary perfusion pressure is judged in the relaxation phase between compressions, not at the peak of the push. Why does myocardial flow depend on letting go?
questions.answer: The compression generates aortic pressure, but the coronary gradient is aortic pressure minus right atrial pressure while the chest is released. Incomplete recoil leaves right atrial pressure high, so the gradient collapses even if the push looked deep.
questions.reasoning: Coronary arteries are perfused by the pressure remaining in the aorta after a compression, opposed by right atrial pressure. Leaning on the chest keeps intrathoracic and right atrial pressure up, which shrinks that difference. Recoil is part of creating coronary flow, not a rest from CPR. The same compressions are what cerebral blood flow depends on, so a poor gradient fails both organs.

questions.prompt: A compressor is going at about 140 per minute and the chest is not coming all the way back. Why is that not more perfusion just because there are more compressions?
questions.answer: Rates of 100 to 120 per minute, with full recoil, are the range associated with better survival. Faster compressions tend to sacrifice depth and recoil, and leaning lowers coronary perfusion pressure.
questions.reasoning: Observational work has favored survival at compression rates of about 100 to 119 per minute over both slower and faster rates. Each compression has to be deep enough and then released. Too fast, depth and release velocity fall. Incomplete recoil keeps right atrial pressure high, so extra compressions do not add coronary or cerebral flow. Quality of the gradient beats a higher count of shallow, unretracted pushes.

principles.title: Perfusion pressure collapses when compressions stop
principles.explanation: Coronary perfusion pressure falls almost immediately when chest compressions pause, and it takes a run of compressions to rebuild. Chest compression fraction is the share of the resuscitation during which compressions are actually happening. A fraction of at least 60% is the minimum the 2025 adult BLS guidance treats as associated with better outcomes; high-performing teams often get above 80%. Some pauses are required: two breaths in 30:2 CPR, a rhythm or pulse check, and delivery of a shock. Those pauses have to be few and short. Professionals often take longer than 10 seconds to decide whether a pulse is present, and the instruction is to start compressions if a pulse is not definitely felt within about 10 seconds. The perishock pause, the gap just before and after a shock, is especially costly. Two randomized trials found no survival benefit from pausing after a shock to inspect the rhythm before restarting CPR, and not restarting promptly is associated with less return of spontaneous circulation. Change compressors about every 2 minutes, or sooner if they are tiring, and do the swap at a planned rhythm check so it does not add a pause of its own.

questions.prompt: The team stops compressions for 20 seconds to feel carefully for a pulse and study the monitor. What happens to coronary perfusion pressure, and why is the pause not free?
questions.answer: It falls almost immediately. Forward coronary flow is gone until compressions rebuild the aortic-minus-right-atrial gradient, and the long check also cuts the chest compression fraction.
questions.reasoning: Aortic diastolic pressure during CPR is generated by compressions and decays as soon as they stop. A careful but prolonged pulse check therefore buys little diagnostic certainty at a high perfusion cost. Professionals are directed to begin compressions when a pulse is not definitely palpated within about 10 seconds. Necessary pauses still happen, but they have to be short enough that most of the resuscitation is hands-on time.

questions.prompt: Immediately after a shock, someone says to hold compressions and watch whether it worked. Why do you put hands back on the chest instead?
questions.answer: The shock has either terminated VF or pulseless VT or it has not. Watching does not perfuse the myocardium. Resume compressions at once and make the next rhythm check at the end of the two-minute cycle.
questions.reasoning: The seconds around a shock are a perishock pause, which is when coronary perfusion pressure is already gone. Trials that paused after defibrillation to analyze the rhythm did not improve survival, and failure to restart compressions promptly is associated with less ROSC. Much of the VF seen at the next scheduled pause is recurrence during CPR, not a reason to have stayed off the chest to look.

principles.title: Shockable rhythms are treated by early defibrillation
principles.explanation: Pulseless ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation are electrically active rhythms that do not eject a stroke volume. The treatment that terminates them is a shock, and it works best early. In the ARREST registry of witnessed out-of-hospital arrest with an initial rhythm of VF, first-shock success was about 93% when the shock came within 6 minutes and about 75% when it was delayed past 16 minutes, and each minute of delay to the first shock was associated with about a 6% lower probability of survival to discharge. If VF has already been prolonged, myocardial energy stores are depleted and CPR before the shock can make defibrillation more effective. The 2025 ALS guidelines prefer a single shock to stacked shocks, then immediate CPR for about 2 minutes. Use a biphasic defibrillator when one is available, at the manufacturer's energy. If that energy is unknown, the maximal dose on that device may be used; the algorithm gives a typical biphasic initial range of 120 to 200 joules as an example. A monophasic device, if that is all you have, is set at 360 joules. Later shocks are at least that same energy, and a higher energy may be considered when the device can escalate and a perfusing rhythm has not returned. The usefulness of pad vector change and double sequential defibrillation for VF that is still present after three or more shocks has not been established. Fix pad contact, pad position, and CPR quality before adding an unproven second technique.

questions.prompt: A monitored patient loses a pulse and the screen shows ventricular fibrillation. Why is the first treatment a shock rather than epinephrine?
questions.answer: Defibrillation is what terminates VF, and delay to the first shock costs survival. Epinephrine is for after initial shocks have failed, not instead of the first shock.
questions.reasoning: Epinephrine can raise aortic diastolic pressure, but it does not organize VF or pulseless VT. The 2025 ALS recommendation is to give epinephrine in a shockable rhythm after initial defibrillation attempts have failed, then 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes. In witnessed, monitored VF the immediate action is one shock and an immediate return to compressions.

questions.prompt: The first rhythm check, after several minutes of CPR for an unwitnessed arrest, is VF. Why not deliver stacked shocks at the highest energy before anyone touches the chest again?
questions.answer: Deliver one shock at the device's recommended biphasic energy, or its maximum if that setting is unknown, then resume CPR for about 2 minutes. A single-shock strategy is preferred because stacked shocks extend the time off the chest.
questions.reasoning: CPR already in progress has been restoring the myocardial substrate that a delayed shock needs. Staying off the chest for shock after shock drops coronary perfusion pressure and ignores the preference for a single shock followed by compressions. If a later shock is required and the defibrillator can escalate, a higher energy may be considered. Vector change and double sequential defibrillation are not established treatments for VF that persists after three or more standard shocks.

principles.title: Many arrests continue until a reversible cause is treated
principles.explanation: Not every arrest is a primary electrical failure. Pulseless electrical activity and asystole often mean the heart cannot beat through a volume, oxygen, metabolic, toxic, or mechanical problem. The 2025 adult cardiac arrest algorithm keeps one reversible-cause list: hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo- or hyperkalemia, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, toxins, pulmonary thrombosis, and coronary thrombosis. Compressions and epinephrine do not drain a tamponade, decompress a tension pneumothorax, or open an occluded coronary artery. Search for these while compressions continue. Point-of-care ultrasound may be used by an experienced operator to look for a reversible cause only when it does not interrupt CPR. Calcium and sodium bicarbonate are not routine drugs for undifferentiated cardiac arrest. Randomized and registry evidence does not show a survival benefit, and routine calcium has a signal toward harm. Both drugs are reserved for specific situations such as hyperkalemia or selected poisonings, which are covered as special circumstances rather than given because the resuscitation has lasted a long time.

questions.prompt: The monitor shows a slow organized rhythm and there is no pulse. Why is another milligram of epinephrine an incomplete plan?
questions.answer: Epinephrine is still indicated early in a nonshockable rhythm, but PEA is often the surface of a cause on the H and T list. That cause has to be found and treated while CPR continues.
questions.reasoning: A vasopressor can raise coronary perfusion pressure. It cannot refill an empty heart, relieve tamponade, decompress a tension pneumothorax, or clear a massive pulmonary embolus or an occluded coronary artery. The algorithm lists those causes because the rhythm will not become a pulse until the obstruction or the metabolic problem is addressed. Epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes and the search happen together; neither replaces the other.

questions.prompt: Someone asks for calcium and sodium bicarbonate because the arrest has gone on a long time. What is the default answer, and what would change it?
questions.answer: Do not give either drug just because time has passed. Routine calcium and routine sodium bicarbonate are not recommended. Give them when a specific indication is present, such as hyperkalemia or a relevant poisoning.
questions.reasoning: Trials and registry data have not shown better survival from routine use in undifferentiated arrest, and routine calcium leans toward harm. A long resuscitation is a reason to recheck CPR quality and the H and T list, not an indication by itself. The guidelines point these drugs at the special circumstances where the mechanism matches.

principles.title: Oxygenate and ventilate without hyperventilation
principles.explanation: Compressions move blood, and that blood still has to carry oxygen while carbon dioxide is cleared. Arterial oxygen content falls if ventilation is left out for a long time, especially in asphyxial arrest. For health care professionals, the 2025 BLS guidance says it is reasonable to give both compressions and ventilations, with enough tidal volume to see the chest rise, while avoiding hypoventilation and hyperventilation. Without an advanced airway the ratio is 30 compressions to 2 breaths. With an advanced airway in place, give 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths per minute) without pausing compressions. Begin with a bag-mask and oxygen. If placing an advanced airway will interrupt compressions, defer it until initial CPR and defibrillation have failed, or until there is ROSC. Hyperventilation undoes the perfusion you just created: extra positive-pressure breaths raise mean intrathoracic pressure, impede venous return, and can erase coronary perfusion pressure. When an endotracheal tube is used, continuous waveform capnography plus clinical assessment is the most reliable confirmation that it is in the trachea. During CPR, end-tidal CO2 is also a surrogate for pulmonary blood flow. A low or falling value is a prompt to reassess compression quality and tube position. Do not use end-tidal CO2 alone to stop resuscitation. In an intubated adult, failure to exceed 10 mm Hg after 20 minutes of ALS may be one part of a multimodal decision to stop. A sudden rise can accompany ROSC, but there is no single cutoff that proves it.

questions.prompt: The trachea is intubated and the bag is being squeezed every 2 or 3 seconds so the patient gets more oxygen. What does that do to coronary perfusion?
questions.answer: That is roughly 20 to 30 breaths per minute. The extra positive-pressure breaths raise intrathoracic pressure, reduce venous return, and lower the coronary perfusion pressure the compressor is generating. With an advanced airway the rate is 1 breath every 6 seconds, enough to see the chest rise.
questions.reasoning: Oxygen delivery does not require that rate. Ten breaths per minute at a tidal volume that lifts the chest oxygenates without holding the chest at high pressure. Faster ventilation subtracts from venous return, so it fights the coronary gradient instead of supporting it. Continued after ROSC, the same excess also lowers PaCO2 and constricts cerebral arterioles. During the arrest the immediate harm is to preload and coronary perfusion.

questions.prompt: End-tidal CO2 has fallen from 18 mm Hg to 8 mm Hg and the team starts discussing whether to stop. What do you check before that discussion?
questions.answer: CPR quality and airway position: rate, depth, recoil, interruptions, and that the tube is still in the trachea. A falling end-tidal CO2 during CPR is a blood-flow signal. It is not a standalone reason to stop.
questions.reasoning: If ventilation is steady, end-tidal CO2 during CPR tracks pulmonary blood flow. A fall often means compressions are no longer moving blood, or the airway has moved. The guidelines say end-tidal CO2 is not used in isolation to end a resuscitation. Only in an intubated patient, and only after 20 minutes of ALS, may failure to exceed 10 mm Hg be considered as one element among others. A sudden rise can be a clue to ROSC, not a cue to stop looking at the patient.

principles.title: After ROSC the brain and heart are vulnerable to a second injury
principles.explanation: A pulse means you are no longer manufacturing blood pressure by hand. It starts ischemia-reperfusion. The myocardium is often stunned, vascular tone is abnormal, and the brain may not autoregulate, so ordinary blood pressure and blood gases can still injure it. The 2025 post-cardiac arrest recommendations stay inside ranges that trials have actually compared. Give 100% oxygen until SpO2 or PaO2 can be measured reliably, because turning the oxygen down before you have a number causes hypoxemia. Once saturation is trustworthy, titrate the inspired oxygen fraction to an SpO2 of 90% to 98% (PaO2 about 60 to 105 mm Hg) and avoid both hypoxemia and hyperoxemia. Keep PaCO2 in a normal physiologic range, generally 35 to 45 mm Hg. Mild hypercapnia did not improve six-month neurologic outcome in the TAME trial. Avoid hypotension by holding mean arterial pressure at least 65 mm Hg. Randomized comparisons of higher versus lower MAP targets have not shown better survival or neurologic outcome, and aiming below 65 mm Hg has not been shown to be safe in this group. Record a 12-lead ECG as soon as feasible. An immediate post-ROSC tracing can over-call ST elevation, and the absence of ST elevation does not exclude an intervenable coronary lesion. For adults who remain unresponsive to verbal commands, a deliberate temperature-control strategy is recommended, holding a temperature between 32 °C and 37.5 °C. Continuing that control for at least 36 hours is reasonable. Do not rewarm faster than 0.5 °C per hour. Routine rapid infusion of cold intravenous fluid for prehospital cooling is not recommended.

questions.prompt: Two minutes after ROSC the pulse oximeter has no reliable reading, and someone turns the oxygen down to avoid oxygen toxicity. Why is that the wrong order?
questions.answer: Until SpO2 or PaO2 is reliably measured, 100% oxygen is recommended. Hyperoxemia is handled by titration after you have a number. Early reduction is what produces hypoxemia.
questions.reasoning: The EXACT trial found more hypoxemic events when oxygen was reduced early toward a lower saturation target. Hyperoxemia can add oxidative injury in reperfused tissue, which is why the target becomes 90% to 98% once measurement is trustworthy. A failed oximeter is not a measurement. You cannot chase the narrower target until the number exists.

questions.prompt: The patient is comatose after ROSC, mean arterial pressure is 58 mm Hg, and the ventilator has been set to a PaCO2 of 28 mm Hg to protect the brain. Which of those protects the brain?
questions.answer: Neither. A MAP below 65 mm Hg is hypotension to correct, and a PaCO2 of 28 mm Hg is hypocapnia, which constricts cerebral arterioles. The targets are a MAP of at least 65 mm Hg and a PaCO2 generally of 35 to 45 mm Hg, plus temperature control when the patient is not responding to voice.
questions.reasoning: After arrest, impaired autoregulation means a low MAP is transmitted as low cerebral blood flow, and a low PaCO2 lowers cerebral blood flow further. Trials have not shown better outcomes from pushing MAP well above 65 mm Hg, so the instruction is a floor of 65 mm Hg rather than a higher invented target or permission to remain below it. Normocapnia, not hyperventilation, is the ventilatory goal. Temperature is then held between 32 °C and 37.5 °C, for at least 36 hours if the patient stays unresponsive to verbal commands.

treatmentApproach.title: Start high-quality chest compressions
treatmentApproach.action: As soon as cardiac arrest is recognized, start compressions on a firm surface. Use a rate of 100 to 120 per minute, a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm), and full chest recoil without leaning. Do not treat depths greater than about 6 cm (2.4 inches) as a better compression. Change the compressor about every 2 minutes, or sooner if they are tiring, and make the change at a rhythm check.
treatmentApproach.why: Coronary and cerebral blood flow during arrest are produced by these compressions. The relaxation-phase gradient that perfuses the heart decays as soon as they stop, and it sags when recoil is incomplete or the compressor fatigues. Rotating at the planned 2-minute check keeps depth up without adding a separate pause.

treatmentApproach.title: Keep pauses short and shared
treatmentApproach.action: Limit a pulse check to about 10 seconds, and start compressions if no definite pulse is felt. Put rhythm analysis, ventilator breaths, and the compressor change into the same pause when you can. Aim for a chest compression fraction of at least 60%, and higher when the team can sustain it.
treatmentApproach.why: An unplanned pause drops coronary perfusion pressure immediately and lowers the fraction of time blood is moving. One short, shared pause costs less than several small ones scattered through the cycle.

treatmentApproach.title: Defibrillate VF and pulseless VT early
treatmentApproach.action: Attach a monitor-defibrillator as soon as it is available. If the rhythm is VF or pulseless VT, deliver one biphasic shock at the manufacturer's energy, or at the device maximum if that energy is unknown. Use 360 joules if the only device is monophasic. Resume compressions immediately. Prefer this single shock to stacked shocks. On later shocks, use at least the same energy, and consider a higher energy if the device can escalate and there is still no pulse. In witnessed, monitored VF, do not delay the first shock for a drug or an intubation.
treatmentApproach.why: A shock is what terminates VF and pulseless VT, and survival falls as the first shock is delayed. Compressions immediately afterward rebuild the perfusion pressure the shock just interrupted. Epinephrine and airway placement do not replace that first shock.

treatmentApproach.title: Oxygenate and ventilate without hyperventilating
treatmentApproach.action: Open the airway and ventilate with a bag-mask and oxygen, using a tidal volume that produces visible chest rise. Without an advanced airway, use 30 compressions and 2 breaths. If an advanced airway is in place, give 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 per minute) and do not pause compressions for the breath. Defer advanced-airway placement when it would interrupt compressions, until initial CPR and defibrillation have failed or ROSC has occurred. Confirm an endotracheal tube with continuous waveform capnography and clinical assessment. If end-tidal CO2 is low or falling, reassess CPR quality and tube position before you reassess prognosis.
treatmentApproach.why: Blood moved by compressions still has to carry oxygen, but extra breaths raise intrathoracic pressure and steal venous return, which removes the coronary gradient those compressions created. Airway insertion and a long look at the capnograph are interruptions unless they stay off the early CPR and defibrillation path.

treatmentApproach.title: Give epinephrine on a rhythm-specific clock
treatmentApproach.action: Get IV or IO access without stopping compressions. Give epinephrine 1 mg IV or IO every 3 to 5 minutes. In asystole or PEA, give the first dose as soon as feasible. In VF or pulseless VT, give it after initial defibrillation attempts have failed, not before the first shock. Do not use high-dose epinephrine. Vasopressin, alone or combined with epinephrine, offers no advantage as a substitute.
treatmentApproach.why: Epinephrine's alpha effect raises aortic diastolic pressure and can therefore raise the coronary perfusion pressure compressions are generating. In a shockable rhythm that dose waits until shocks have been tried, because the rhythm itself is the problem defibrillation treats. Placing the line and giving the drug must not create an extra pause.

treatmentApproach.title: Add an antiarrhythmic only for shock-refractory VF or pulseless VT
treatmentApproach.action: If VF or pulseless VT continues after defibrillation, amiodarone or lidocaine may be considered. Amiodarone is 300 mg IV or IO, then 150 mg if a second dose is needed. Lidocaine is 1 to 1.5 mg/kg IV or IO, then 0.5 to 0.75 mg/kg. Do not give calcium or sodium bicarbonate as routine arrest drugs.
treatmentApproach.why: These antiarrhythmics are an adjunct for a shockable rhythm that defibrillation has not settled. They are not treatment for PEA or asystole, and they do not replace further shocks or CPR. Calcium and bicarbonate do not improve undifferentiated arrest; they are reserved for specific reversible causes such as hyperkalemia or selected poisonings.

treatmentApproach.title: Search for Hs and Ts while CPR continues
treatmentApproach.action: During compressions, look for hypovolemia, hypoxia, acidosis, hypo- or hyperkalemia, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, toxins, pulmonary thrombosis, and coronary thrombosis, and treat the cause you find. Use ultrasound only if the operator is experienced and the probe does not stop compressions.
treatmentApproach.why: A mechanical or metabolic cause will not yield to compressions and epinephrine alone. The search is part of resuscitation, but it is not a reason to let coronary perfusion pressure fall to zero while people look.

treatmentApproach.title: Limit secondary injury after ROSC
treatmentApproach.action: When a pulse returns, leave 100% oxygen on until SpO2 or PaO2 is reliably measured, then titrate to an SpO2 of 90% to 98%. Ventilate toward a PaCO2 of about 35 to 45 mm Hg. Correct hypotension so mean arterial pressure is at least 65 mm Hg. Record a 12-lead ECG as soon as feasible. If the patient does not respond to verbal commands, control temperature between 32 °C and 37.5 °C. Continuing that control for at least 36 hours is reasonable, and it is reasonable to avoid rewarming faster than 0.5 °C per hour. Do not give a routine prehospital bolus of cold intravenous fluid to force hypothermia.
treatmentApproach.why: After ROSC the problem changes from no flow to reperfusion. Hypoxemia, hyperoxemia, hypocapnia, hypotension, and uncontrolled temperature each add injury to a brain that may not be autoregulating. These are the ranges and floors from the 2025 post-cardiac arrest guideline, including the shift from the ventilation limits used during CPR to a normal PaCO2 once a pulse has returned.
